 RAP charges 1% to 10% of income, with a $10 minimum and forgiveness at 30 years. See how it compares with IBR, PAYE, ICR and SAVE
 1 / 9 List slides The new Repayment Assistance Plan vs. the old student loan plans, compared List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 26, 2026 Add QZ to Google Pang Yuhao / Unsplash
 Federal student loan repayment looks different this fall than it did a year ago. A court order ended the SAVE plan in March, the Repayment Assistance Plan, known as RAP, opened for enrollment on July 1, and borrowers with older loans now have to choose between plans that remain and plans that are on a clock to disappear.
 The terms below come from the pages Federal Student Aid's loan servicers publish for each plan, including Edfinancial Services' RAP page . The July 1, 2028 end dates for PAYE and ICR come from analyses of the 2025 law that created RAP. The seven slides cover how RAP works, how it compares with IBR, SAVE, PAYE and ICR, what decides which plan costs less and the deadlines that matter.
 How RAP works 
 Towfiqu barbhuiya / Unsplash
 RAP sets your payment as a percentage of your adjusted gross income, from 1% to 10%, then divides it by 12. Income up to $10,000 pays a flat $120 a year, or $10 a month. Each additional $10,000 of income up to $100,000 raises the rate by one percentage point, and income above $100,000 pays 10%. Each dependent you claim on your tax return reduces the monthly payment by $50, but it can't fall below $10.
 By that formula, $30,000 in income falls in the 2% bracket, or $50 a month, $60,000 falls in the 5% bracket, or $250 a month, and $120,000 pays 10%, or $1,000 a month, all before any dependent reduction.
 RAP covers Direct Loans, including Direct PLUS loans made to graduate or professional students and Direct Consolidation loans that don't include a Parent PLUS loan. When your payment doesn't cover the monthly interest, the unpaid interest is subsidized, and the Education Department adds a matching principal payment, up to $50, when your payment doesn't reduce your principal by at least that much. Any balance left after 30 years, or 360 months, is forgiven, and Public Service Loan Forgiveness is available after 10 years.
 RAP vs. IBR 
 Kelly Sikkema / Unsplash
 Income-Based Repayment sets your payment at 10% or 15% of discretionary income, depending on when you took your first loans, where discretionary income is your income above 150% of the poverty line for your family size. Your payment never exceeds what you'd pay under the 10-year standard plan, and any balance is forgiven after 20 or 25 years. RAP uses all of your income, has no such cap and forgives after 30 years, so higher earners can pay more under RAP than under IBR.
 Two features favor RAP. It covers unpaid interest on any eligible loan, while IBR covers it only on subsidized loans and only for the first three years, and RAP's principal match has no IBR equivalent. Low earners face a tradeoff, since IBR can produce a $0 payment while RAP never falls below $10, according to AccessLex. IBR is also the only income-driven plan that accepts older FFEL loans, and neither plan accepts Direct Parent PLUS loans.
 RAP vs. SAVE 
 Etienne Boulanger / Unsplash
 SAVE is gone. A court order ended it on March 10, 2026, and borrowers who were enrolled get a notice from their servicer sometime between July 1 and August 15, then have 90 days from the date of that notice to pick another plan. Counting from those dates, the deadlines fall between about September 29 and November 13, 2026.
 SAVE set payments at 5% to 10% of income above 225% of the poverty line, and unlike RAP it had no minimum payment. RAP bases payments on all of your income, with a $10 floor.
 RAP vs. PAYE 
 Dragos Blaga / Unsplash
 PAYE is the closest older match to IBR for newer borrowers. Payments are 10% of discretionary income, capped at the 10-year standard amount, with forgiveness after 20 years. It was open to people who were new borrowers on or after October 1, 2007 and who received a Direct Loan on or after October 1, 2011.
 Effective July 1, 2026, PAYE's interest subsidy covers unpaid interest on subsidized loans for the first three consecutive years of repayment. PAYE is being phased out and is scheduled to end by July 1, 2028, so borrowers who stay on it will eventually need to move to IBR or RAP.
 RAP vs. ICR 
 Kelly Sikkema / Unsplash
 Income-Contingent Repayment is the oldest income-driven plan and, for most borrowers, the most expensive. The payment is the lesser of 20% of discretionary income, here income above 100% of the poverty line, or what you'd pay on a fixed 12-year plan adjusted for income, and any balance is forgiven after 25 years.
 ICR's distinguishing feature is that Direct Consolidation loans that include Parent PLUS loans can use it, which makes it the only income-driven route for those borrowers. RAP excludes them. ICR is also scheduled to end by July 1, 2028, and Parent PLUS loans first disbursed on or after July 1, 2026 can't use ICR or RAP.
 What decides which plan costs less 
 Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash
 Each plan's formula points to who tends to pay less. RAP's tiers apply to all of your income, with a $10 floor and no cap, so payments keep rising with earnings, to 10% of income above $100,000. IBR protects the income below 150% of the poverty line and stops at the standard 10-year payment, which tends to help people with large balances and modest incomes.
 RAP's $50 monthly reduction per dependent and its interest waiver help families and borrowers whose payment is smaller than the interest, while IBR's 20-year clock, against RAP's 30, matters most to people who expect to reach forgiveness. Public Service Loan Forgiveness comes after 10 years under both, and forgiven balances may be taxed as income. StudentAid.gov's repayment calculator shows the payment under each plan.
 Deadlines and who has to choose 
 Towfiqu barbhuiya / Unsplash
 Loans first disbursed on or after July 1, 2026 can use only RAP for income-driven repayment, along with a new standard plan whose length depends on the balance: 10 years under $25,000, 15 years from $25,000 to $49,999, 20 years from $50,000 to $99,999 and 25 years at $100,000 or more.
 Borrowers with older loans can choose between RAP and IBR, which remains available, and PAYE and ICR are scheduled to end by July 1, 2028. RAP is available only for Direct Loans, and you can apply on StudentAid.gov.
 This article is for informational purposes only and is not financial advice. Plan terms and deadlines can change, so confirm them with your servicer and StudentAid.gov.
